entries.excerpt: So he walked with her through the devious ways of the west side of the town, and through the bustle of gathering nightfall in populous streets, to the quiet precinct of Washington Square. They lingered a moment at the foot of Dr. Sloper’s white marble steps, above which a spotless white door, adorned with a glittering silver plate, seemed to figure, for Morris, the closed portal of happiness; and then Mrs. Penniman’s companion rested a melancholy eye upon a lighted window in the upper part of the house.
entries.note: James moves from the crowded streets into a quiet square. The white door of the fictional Sloper house becomes a boundary between Morris Townsend and the life he hopes to enter.
entries.precision: Area described. The pin marks the square, not an identified address for the fictional house.
entries.visit_note: Explore the square and its north-side streets from public paths.

entries.map_query: Metropolitan Museum of Art New York
entries.excerpt: Avoiding the popular "Wolfe collection," whose anecdotic canvases filled one of the main galleries of the queer wilderness of cast-iron and encaustic tiles known as the Metropolitan Museum, they had wandered down a passage to the room where the "Cesnola antiquities" mouldered in unvisited loneliness.
entries.note: Archer and Ellen find privacy among antiquities. Wharton makes the museum feel secluded and faintly melancholy, a refuge from the social scrutiny outside.
entries.precision: Named institution. The historical gallery arrangement in the novel is not a guide to the museum today.
entries.visit_note: The museum is at 1000 Fifth Avenue. Check admission and opening hours before visiting.

entries.map_query: Ed Koch Queensboro Bridge New York
entries.excerpt: Over the great bridge, with the sunlight through the girders making a constant flicker upon the moving cars, with the city rising up across the river in white heaps and sugar lumps all built with a wish out of nonolfactory money. The city seen from the Queensboro Bridge is always the city seen for the first time, in its first wild promise of all the mystery and the beauty in the world.
entries.note: Nick approaches Manhattan with Gatsby. The bridge turns the familiar skyline into a promise of reinvention, just as Gatsby is presenting his own story.
entries.precision: Named bridge. The pin identifies the crossing, not a precise viewpoint or pedestrian entrance.
entries.visit_note: Use Google Maps for a current pedestrian approach; the passage describes a journey by car.

entries.locator: Chapter IV, after Jordan’s story at the Plaza
entries.excerpt: When Jordan Baker had finished telling all this we had left the Plaza for half an hour and were driving in a victoria through Central Park. The sun had gone down behind the tall apartments of the movie stars in the West Fifties, and the clear voices of children, already gathered like crickets on the grass, rose through the hot twilight:
entries.excerpt_kind: Paragraph leading into a quoted song
entries.note: After Jordan tells Nick about Daisy and Gatsby, the city softens into evening. Children’s voices and a carriage ride briefly replace the novel’s parties and display.
entries.precision: Area described. The novel gives no exact carriage route; the pin marks the park’s southern edge.
entries.visit_note: Start at Central Park South. The text does not identify a particular path.

entries.excerpt: There now is your insular city of the Manhattoes, belted round by wharves as Indian isles by coral reefs—commerce surrounds it with her surf. Right and left, the streets take you waterward. Its extreme downtown is the battery, where that noble mole is washed by waves, and cooled by breezes, which a few hours previous were out of sight of land. Look at the crowds of water-gazers there.
entries.note: Before Ishmael goes to sea, he watches New Yorkers drawn to the waterfront. The Battery becomes the city’s threshold to an ocean that seems to pull people out of their everyday lives.
entries.precision: Area described. The pin is on the present-day waterfront; the shoreline has changed since Melville wrote.
entries.visit_note: Follow the public waterfront paths; this is not a reconstructed nineteenth-century viewpoint.

entries.locator: “The Cop and the Anthem,” opening paragraph
entries.excerpt: On his bench in Madison Square Soapy moved uneasily. When wild geese honk high of nights, and when women without sealskin coats grow kind to their husbands, and when Soapy moves uneasily on his bench in the park, you may know that winter is near at hand.
entries.note: The park bench is Soapy’s home, and the first signs of winter are an urgent problem. O. Henry measures the changing season from the perspective of someone who has nowhere warm to go.
entries.precision: Named park. Soapy’s bench is fictional and has no identified present-day location.
entries.visit_note: Visit the public park between Fifth Avenue, Madison Avenue, 23rd and 26th Streets.

entries.map_query: Fulton Ferry Landing Brooklyn New York
entries.locator: “Crossing Brooklyn Ferry,” section 1; later collected text
entries.excerpt:
Flood-tide below me! I see you face to face!
Clouds of the west—sun there half an hour high—I see you also face to face.
Crowds of men and women attired in the usual costumes, how curious you are to me!
On the ferry-boats the hundreds and hundreds that cross, returning home, are more curious to me than you suppose,
And you that shall cross from shore to shore years hence are more to me, and more in my meditations, than you might suppose.
entries.note: Whitman looks at commuters on the river and addresses people who will cross it long after him. The shared view becomes a connection between strangers across generations.
entries.precision: Historical crossing. The pin marks the Brooklyn landing associated with the Fulton Ferry, not the poet’s exact position.
entries.visit_note: Read from the public waterfront. The old crossing and today’s ferry services are different.

entries.map_query: McSorleys Old Ale House 15 East 7th Street New York
entries.locator: Opening sentence; The New Yorker, April 13, 1940 issue
entries.excerpt: McSorley’s occupies the ground floor of a red brick tenement at 15 Seventh Street, just off Cooper Square, where the Bowery ends.
entries.note: Mitchell begins with the building and the street. His profile makes a neighborhood saloon the subject of close observation, preserving the texture of an ordinary New York gathering place.
entries.precision: Named venue and street address. The description belongs to the 1940 article, not a report on the bar today.
entries.visit_note: 15 East 7th Street. Check the venue’s current visitor information before going.
